metadata.title: Posters and flyers
metadata.series: Humanitarians AI — how to use AI

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. You need a poster — a garage sale, a bake sale, your side business. The AI can't design it. But it can do the next best thing: draw the art. You do the words.

beats.narration_text: Four terms. Image generator: an app that turns your words into pictures. Prompt: the sentence you type. Printable: a file sharp enough to print. Aspect ratio: the picture's shape — tall, wide, or square. That's the vocabulary.

terms.meaning: an app that turns words into pictures
a file sharp enough to print
the picture's shape — tall, wide, square

beats.narration_text: Here's the job. A poster is just a big piece of paper with three jobs: a headline people read across the room, the details they read up close, and a picture that makes them look. You bring the first two. The AI does the third.

beats.narration_text: The picture part is our sister film's job. Pictures from words taught the ladder: start vague, add subject plus style plus mood, then iterate — like texting a friend. And the five-slot recipe: subject, setting, style, lighting, mood. Go watch it if you missed it. Here, we just use it.

beats.narration_text: Step one: tell it the real job first. Before any picture, write down three facts: what — a garage sale; when — Saturday, nine in the morning; where — twelve Maple Street. The AI needs these because the poster needs these. No facts, no poster.

beats.narration_text: Step two: make the words exact. Type the exact headline you want, in quotes: 'GARAGE SALE'. The generator draws letters as shapes — it doesn't type them — so it misspells. Check every letter. Your headline is your shop sign; a misspelled sign costs you customers.

beats.narration_text: Step three: ask for the layout. Big headline on top, details below, and leave the bottom half empty — that's where your facts go. If you let the picture fill the whole page, there's nowhere left for the words, and a poster without words is just wallpaper.

beats.narration_text: And here's the pro move: split the job. Have the AI draw a picture with no words in it at all — a warm morning garage scene, no text. Then you add the headline and details yourself, in any simple poster tool. AI pictures, your words. The letters are always spelled right, because a human typed them.

beats.narration_text: Then the print checklist — three checks before you print a hundred. One: tall shape, the way paper is. Two: dark words on light paper — it reads from across the room. Three: the three-second test. Hold it at arm's length. Headline, when, where — can a stranger get all three in three seconds? If not, make the headline bigger.

shot.visual_intent: The poster stands center; three terracotta checks land one by one with short labels: 'tall shape', 'dark on light', '3-second test'.

beats.narration_text: One last rule: say it's AI-made. Most apps that make pictures offer an AI label — use it. The label matters most when the picture could pass for a real photo, and on a flyer for your business, honesty is the whole brand.

beats.narration_text: The recap. One: say the real job — what, when, where. Two: make the words exact, in quotes. Three: AI draws the picture, you add the words. Four: run the three checks and label it AI-made. That is a poster in an afternoon.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm making a flyer for [your event — what, when, where]. Give me the five-slot picture recipe — subject, setting, style, lighting, mood — for a background with no text in the image, plus one short headline I can add myself. Then two checks yourself. One: does the picture contain any words at all? If it does, ask again for no text. Two: read your poster from across the room — headline, when, where, three seconds.
